modules.title: Hello, C
modules.summary: Your first programs. What main() is, how printf prints text, and how to read the compiler's complaints.

steps.title: Your first program
steps.text:
A **program** is a list of instructions the computer follows from top to bottom. C is a *compiled* language: you write the instructions as text (the **source code**), a tool called the **compiler** checks them and translates them into machine code the processor can run, and then the program runs. Every time you press **Check**, a real C compiler does exactly that in your browser.

### The shape of every C program

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("Hi!\n");
    return 0;
}
```

```text
Hi!
```

Line by line:

- `#include <stdio.h>` pulls in the **st**andar**d** **i**nput/**o**utput library. It tells the compiler what `printf` is. Without it the compiler doesn't know the name and reports an error.
- `int main(void)` starts a **function** called `main`. Every C program begins running at `main`, no matter how big it is. `int` says it gives back a whole number when it finishes, and `(void)` says it takes no inputs.
- The curly braces `{ }` hold the function's **body**: the instructions that run, in order.
- `printf("Hi!\n");` calls the `printf` function to print text. The text goes inside double quotes. `\n` is a *newline*: it ends the line, like pressing Enter.
- `return 0;` ends `main` and reports "success" (0) to the operating system. A non-zero number would mean something went wrong.

### Common mistakes

- **Spelling and capitals matter.** `Printf` or `print` are different names, and the compiler will say something like `call to undeclared function 'print'`.
- **Forgetting `#include <stdio.h>`** gives a similar error about `printf`.
- **Forgetting the `;`** at the end of a statement. You'll practice reading that error in step 5.

**Your turn:** fill in the blank so the program prints `Hello, World!`.
hints: The function that prints text is spelled `printf` (print formatted).

steps.title: Printing your own text
steps.text:
A piece of text in double quotes, like `"I like pizza"`, is called a **string literal**. `printf` prints it **exactly** as written: every letter, space and capital. The double quotes themselves are not printed; they only mark where the text starts and ends.

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("C was created in 1972\n");
    printf("   spaces   are   kept\n");
    return 0;
}
```

```text
C was created in 1972
   spaces   are   kept
```

### Statements and semicolons

Each instruction inside `main` is a **statement**, and in C every statement ends with a semicolon `;`, the way a sentence ends with a period. The compiler uses the semicolons to tell where one instruction stops and the next begins. Line breaks don't matter to it: you could put two statements on one line, but one per line is much easier to read.

### Why exact output matters

The tests on this site compare your program's output with the expected output character by character (ignoring only spaces at the ends of lines and blank lines at the very end). Real programs work the same way: another program reading your output, or a grader at work, won't guess what you meant. `I am learning c` is not the same as `I am learning C`.

**Your turn:** make the program print exactly:

```
I am learning C
```
hints: Type the sentence between the quotes. Capital letters and spaces matter.

steps.title: Several lines
steps.text:
`printf` doesn't start a new line by itself. Each call continues **exactly where the last one stopped**, and only a `\n` moves the cursor to the start of the next line. So these two calls print on the same line:

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("Ready, ");
    printf("set, ");
    printf("go!\n");
    printf("Next line\n");
    return 0;
}
```

```text
Ready, set, go!
Next line
```

Think of the output as a typewriter: the text goes where the cursor is, and `\n` is the carriage return. That means you can build one line from several calls, or print several lines from one call:

```c
printf("one\ntwo\nthree\n");   // three lines from one call
```

Both styles are fine. Programs usually use one `printf` per line because it's easier to read and change.

### The order is the order

Statements in `main` run **top to bottom**, one after another. If you swap two `printf` lines, their output swaps too. This "one step at a time, in order" idea is the foundation for everything that follows: later you'll learn to skip steps (`if`) and repeat them (loops).

### Common mistakes

- Forgetting the `\n` at the end, so the next thing printed is glued to the end of the line.
- Putting `\n` at the *start* instead of the end, which adds a blank line before the text.

**Your turn:** write a program that prints these three lines:

```
Counter-Strike
is a game
about aim
```
hints: Add one `printf` per line. Each one needs `\n` at the end of the text.
The second line is `printf("is a game\n");`

steps.title: Escape sequences
steps.text:
Inside a string, some characters are special. A `"` would end the string early, and there's no key for "new line" that you can put between quotes. C solves this with **escape sequences**: a backslash `\` followed by a character, meaning "the next character is not what it looks like".

| You write | You get |
|---|---|
| `\n` | new line |
| `\t` | tab (jump to the next column) |
| `\"` | a double quote character |
| `\\` | a single backslash |

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("Name\tScore\n");
    printf("Ada\t95\n");
    printf("A path: C:\\games\\cs\n");
    printf("He said \"nice shot\"\n");
    return 0;
}
```

```text
Name	Score
Ada	95
A path: C:\games\cs
He said "nice shot"
```

Each escape sequence is two characters in your source code but becomes **one** character in the output. The compiler does the translation.

### Common mistakes

- Writing `"She said "hi""`: the second `"` ends the string, and the compiler gets confused by what follows. Escape the inner quotes.
- Using a forward slash `/n` instead of a backslash `\n`. That just prints `/n`.
- A single `\` before a normal letter (like `\q`) is not a valid escape, and the compiler warns about it.

**Your turn:** print this line exactly, including the quotes:

```
She said "gg" and left
```
hints: A plain `"` would end the string early. Write `\"` for each quote you want printed.

steps.title: Comments and reading errors
steps.text:
### Comments

Comments are notes for people reading the code. The compiler throws them away, so they never change what the program does.

```c
// A line comment runs from the two slashes to the end of the line.
/* A block comment can
   span several lines. */
printf("hi\n"); // comments can also follow code
```

Good comments explain **why** the code does something ("prices are in cents so we never round"), not what it obviously does.

### Reading compiler errors

When your code isn't valid C, the compiler stops and reports an error. Learning to read these messages is one of the most useful skills in programming. A typical error looks like this:

```text
main.c:4:25: error: expected ';' after expression
```

- `main.c` is the file, `4` is the **line** and `25` the **column** where the compiler noticed the problem.
- `error:` means it can't continue. A `warning:` means the code compiles but is suspicious; take warnings seriously too.
- The message describes what it expected.

One important detail: the compiler reports where it **noticed** the problem, which isn't always where the mistake is. For a missing semicolon, modern compilers point right at the spot where the `;` belongs. But for other mistakes, such as a missing closing quote or `}`, the error can appear a line or more *later*, because that's where the compiler realized something was wrong. If the line it names looks fine, look at the lines just above it.

When there are several errors, **fix the first one first**. One mistake can confuse the compiler into reporting extra errors that disappear once the first is fixed.

On this site, errors also appear in the editor next to the line, with a plain-English explanation below the code.

**Your turn:** this program has two mistakes. Press **Check** first to see what the compiler says, then fix both so it prints `Fixed it` on one line.
hints: The compiler points at the line where it noticed the problem, which is sometimes the line *after* the real mistake.

steps.title: Constants and sizeof
steps.text:
### Constants

Some values should never change while the program runs: the number of players on a team, the length of a round, a tax rate. Put `const` in front of the declaration to make the variable **read-only**:

```c
const int MAX_PLAYERS = 10;
MAX_PLAYERS = 12;   // error: assignment of read-only variable
```

If any later line tries to change it, the program doesn't compile. That turns a silent bug into an error you see immediately. It also documents your intent: a reader knows this value is fixed. Many programmers write constant names in `UPPER_CASE` so they stand out.

### sizeof

Every type takes up a fixed number of **bytes** of memory. The `sizeof` operator tells you how many:

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("char: %zu\n", sizeof(char));
    printf("double: %zu\n", sizeof(double));
    printf("long long: %zu\n", sizeof(long long));
    return 0;
}
```

```text
char: 1
double: 8
long long: 8
```

`sizeof` gives a value of a special unsigned type called `size_t`, and the matching `printf` specifier is `%zu`. A `char` is 1 byte by definition. The others depend on the machine, but on this site and on almost every modern computer an `int` is 4 bytes (so it can hold values up to about 2.1 billion) and a `double` is 8.

Knowing sizes matters once you work with memory directly, which you'll do with arrays and pointers.

**Your turn:** declare a constant `int` named `ROUND_TIME` equal to `115`, and print:

```
Round time: 115
int bytes: 4
```
hints: The keyword that makes a variable read-only is `const`.
`sizeof(int)` gives the size of an int in bytes.

steps.title: The integer division trap
steps.text:
This is one of the most famous traps in C. When **both** sides of `/` are integers, C does **integer division**: it divides and throws the fractional part away. It doesn't round; it just cuts it off (truncates toward zero).

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("%d\n", 7 / 2);
    printf("%d\n", 99 / 100);
    printf("%f\n", 7.0 / 2);
    printf("%f\n", (double)7 / 2);
    return 0;
}
```

```text
3
0
3.500000
3.500000
```

### Why storing into a double doesn't help

```c
double avg = 7 / 2;   // avg is 3.0, not 3.5
```

C works out the right side **first**, using only what's on the right. `7 / 2` is int divided by int, so it becomes 3. Only then is 3 converted to a `double` and stored. The destination's type is never considered while the expression is being evaluated.

### How to get a real division

If **either** side of `/` is a `double`, C converts the other side too and does a real division. You can:

- write a decimal literal: `7.0 / 2`
- **cast** a variable, which means converting its value to another type for this expression: `(double)kills / rounds`

A cast is written as the type in parentheses before the value. `(double)kills` doesn't change the variable `kills`; it produces a `double` copy of its value for this calculation.

Put the cast on one of the operands, not around the whole division: `(double)(kills / rounds)` still does the integer division first, and then converts the already-truncated answer.

**Your turn:** 25 kills over 10 rounds should print `Kills per round: 2.50`. Right now it prints `2.00`. Fix the calculation of `kpr` so it does a real division.

steps.title: Several values at once
steps.text:
One `scanf` call can read several values. List one format specifier per value, and one address per variable, in the same order:

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int width, height;
    scanf("%d %d", &width, &height);
    printf("Area: %d\n", width * height);
    return 0;
}
```

```text
12
5
```

```text
Area: 60
```

### Whitespace is flexible

When reading numbers, `scanf` skips any **whitespace** (spaces, tabs and newlines) before each one. So the program above reads the same values whether they're typed as `12 5` on one line or on two separate lines like in the example. A space in the format string also means "skip any amount of whitespace here", so `"%d %d"` and `"%d%d"` behave the same for numbers.

Other characters in the format string must match the input exactly. With `"%d,%d"` the input has to be `12,5`; if a comma isn't there, reading stops early.

### How scanf reads

Think of the input as a stream of characters with a reading position. Each `%d` skips whitespace, reads digits (and an optional sign) as far as they go, converts them to an int, and moves the position forward. The next `scanf` call continues from there. Reading is always left to right; nothing is read twice.

**Your turn:** read a player's kills and deaths and print their difference.

Input: `18 11` prints `+/-: 7`

steps.title: Reading doubles
steps.text:
Here's a quirk you just have to memorize: `printf` uses `%f` to print a `double`, but `scanf` needs **`%lf`** ("long float") to read one.

| Type | print with | read with |
|---|---|---|
| `int` | `%d` | `%d` |
| `double` | `%f` | `%lf` |
| `char` | `%c` | `%c` |

The reason is history: when you pass a value to `printf`, a `float` is automatically converted to `double`, so `%f` works for both. `scanf` receives an address instead, and it must know whether the box at that address is a 4-byte `float` or an 8-byte `double`. Using `%f` with a `double` writes the wrong number of bytes and gives nonsense.

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    double km;
    scanf("%lf", &km);
    double miles = km * 0.621371;
    printf("%.2f km = %.2f miles\n", km, miles);
    return 0;
}
```

```text
42.195
```

```text
42.20 km = 26.22 miles
```

### Formulas with doubles

When a formula mixes a `double` with int literals, like `km * 0.621371` or `c * 9 / 5 + 32`, C works left to right with precedence: `c * 9` is a double (because `c` is), so `/ 5` is a real division too. The integer-division trap only bites when **both** sides of `/` are ints. If you wrote `9 / 5 * c`, the `9 / 5` would be done first as ints and give 1, which is wrong.

**Your turn:** read a temperature in Celsius and print it in Fahrenheit with one decimal. The formula is `f = c * 9 / 5 + 32`.

Input `100` prints `212.0`. Input `36.6` prints `97.9`.

steps.title: #define constants
steps.text:
Before the compiler proper sees your code, a first stage called the **preprocessor** runs. It handles every line that starts with `#`. You've been using it since the first lesson: `#include <stdio.h>` tells the preprocessor to paste in the contents of that header file.

`#define` creates a **macro**: a name that the preprocessor replaces with text everywhere it appears.

```c
#include <stdio.h>

#define MAX_HP 100
#define GAME_NAME "Arena"

int main(void) {
    int hp = MAX_HP;
    printf("%s: %d/%d\n", GAME_NAME, hp - 35, MAX_HP);
    return 0;
}
```

```text
Arena: 65/100
```

### It's text replacement

The preprocessor doesn't understand C. It literally replaces the token `MAX_HP` with `100` before compiling, as if you had typed `100` yourself. So there's no type, no memory, and no `=` or `;` in the definition. A common mistake is `#define MAX_HP 100;`: the semicolon becomes part of the replacement and breaks expressions like `MAX_HP * 2`.

### Conventions

- Macro names are written in `UPPER_CASE`, so readers know text replacement is happening.
- Use them for values used in many places, so changing one line updates them all.
- In modern C, `const` variables and `enum` constants are often preferable because they have types and obey scope. But `#define` is still everywhere in real C code, including all the standard headers, and it's the only option for some jobs, like conditional compilation (`#ifdef DEBUG`). One C quirk: unlike in C++, a `const int` is not a true compile-time constant in C, so it can't size an array declared outside a function; a `#define` or an `enum` constant can.

**Your turn:** define `TEAM_SIZE` as `5` so the program prints `10 players`.
hints: `#define NAME value`, with no `=` and no semicolon.

steps.title: Macro pitfalls
steps.text:
Macros can take parameters, which makes them look like functions:

```c
#define SQUARE(x) x * x
```

But they aren't functions. The preprocessor pastes the argument's **text** into the body, without evaluating it first. That leads to surprises:

```c
SQUARE(1 + 2)      // becomes  1 + 2 * 1 + 2   which is 5, not 9
100 / SQUARE(5)    // becomes  100 / 5 * 5     which is 100, not 4
```

The fix is to put parentheses around **every use of each parameter** and around **the whole body**:

```c
#include <stdio.h>

#define BAD_SQUARE(x) x * x
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
#define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))

int main(void) {
    printf("%d %d\n", BAD_SQUARE(1 + 2), SQUARE(1 + 2));
    printf("%d %d\n", 100 / BAD_SQUARE(5), 100 / SQUARE(5));
    printf("%d\n", MAX(3, 7) * 2);
    return 0;
}
```

```text
5 9
100 4
14
```

### Another trap: arguments evaluated twice

`MAX(i++, j)` expands to use `i++` twice, so `i` may be incremented twice. A real function evaluates each argument exactly once. This is why modern C code prefers `static inline` functions over function-like macros whenever possible: they have types, evaluate arguments once, and show up in the debugger. Macros remain useful for things functions can't do, but always write them defensively.

**Your turn:** `DOUBLE(3 + 4) * 2` should be 28, but this prints 18. Fix the `DOUBLE` macro.
hints: Expand it by hand: `3 + 4 + 3 + 4 * 2` = 18. The `* 2` only grabbed the last 4.
Wrap the argument and the body: `#define DOUBLE(x) ((x) + (x))`.

require.message: Parenthesize the macro fully: `((x) + (x))`.

steps.title: Flags
steps.text:
A common use of bits is **flags**: packing several yes/no settings into a single integer, one bit each. File permissions, network protocol headers, graphics options and hardware registers all work this way.

Give each flag its own bit with a shift:

```c
#define BOLD      (1u << 0)   /* 001 */
#define ITALIC    (1u << 1)   /* 010 */
#define UNDERLINE (1u << 2)   /* 100 */
```

Then four operations cover everything:

| Goal | Code |
|---|---|
| turn a flag on | `style \|= ITALIC;` |
| turn a flag off | `style &= ~ITALIC;` |
| toggle a flag | `style ^= ITALIC;` |
| test a flag | `if (style & ITALIC)` |

```c
#include <stdio.h>

#define BOLD      (1u << 0)
#define ITALIC    (1u << 1)
#define UNDERLINE (1u << 2)

int main(void) {
    unsigned style = BOLD | UNDERLINE;
    printf("%u\n", style);
    style ^= BOLD;
    style |= ITALIC;
    printf("%u bold=%d italic=%d\n", style, (style & BOLD) != 0, (style & ITALIC) != 0);
    return 0;
}
```

```text
5
6 bold=0 italic=1
```

### Why `&= ~FLAG` turns a flag off

`~ITALIC` has every bit set **except** the italic bit (`...11101`). AND-ing with it keeps every other bit as it was and forces the italic bit to 0.

### Why `!= 0` when testing

`style & ITALIC` is either 0 or the flag's value (here 2), not 1. As a condition in `if` that's fine, since non-zero is true. When you want an actual 0 or 1, compare with `!= 0` (or use `!!`).

Combining flags with `|` when calling a function (like `BOLD | ITALIC`) is a pattern you'll see in many C APIs, including `open()` on Unix.

**Your turn:** fill in the operators.

steps.title: Headers and include guards
steps.text:
Real C programs are thousands or millions of lines, split across many files. Understanding how those files fit together is essential for working on any real codebase.

### Modules: a header and a source file

Each module usually has two files:

- A **header** (`score.h`) with **declarations**: type definitions, function prototypes and constants. It's the module's public interface: what other code may use.
- A **source file** (`score.c`) with the **definitions**: the actual function bodies. It `#include`s its own header.

Other files `#include "score.h"` (quotes for your own headers, angle brackets for system headers) and can then call its functions.

### How it's built

The compiler turns each `.c` file into an **object file** separately, knowing only what its includes declared. Then the **linker** joins all the object files, connecting each call to the matching definition. If a definition is missing, the linker reports an error like `undefined reference to 'kd_ratio'` (or `undefined symbol: kd_ratio`); if something is defined twice, `multiple definition` (or `duplicate symbol`).

### Include guards

`#include` pastes a file's text. Headers often end up included more than once (`main.c` includes `a.h` and `b.h`, and both include `score.h`), and defining the same struct twice is an error. An **include guard** makes repeat inclusions disappear:

```c
#include <stdio.h>

#ifndef GREETING_H
#define GREETING_H
#define GREETING "hi"
typedef struct { int times; } Repeat;
#endif

#ifndef GREETING_H
#define GREETING_H
#define GREETING "hi"
typedef struct { int times; } Repeat;
#endif

int main(void) {
    Repeat r = {2};
    for (int i = 0; i < r.times; i++) printf("%s\n", GREETING);
    return 0;
}
```

```text
hi
hi
```

The first time, `GREETING_H` isn't defined, so everything up to `#endif` is kept, and `GREETING_H` gets defined. The second time, `#ifndef GREETING_H` is false and the preprocessor skips the whole block. Many compilers also accept `#pragma once` at the top of a header for the same effect.

The editor here holds a single file, so this program pastes the "header" in **twice** to simulate a double include. **Your turn:** complete the guard so it compiles.

steps.title: Hello, C++
steps.text:
Welcome to C++. Bjarne Stroustrup started it in 1979 as "C with Classes" and renamed it C++ in 1983, and almost everything you learned in C still works: variables, `if`, loops, functions, pointers, arrays and structs. What C++ adds are tools that make programs **safer** and **shorter**: classes that clean up after themselves, a huge standard library (strings, dynamic arrays, maps, algorithms), references, templates and more.

The first difference you'll notice is output. Instead of `printf` with format specifiers, C++ uses **streams**:

```cpp
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int kills = 25;
    double accuracy = 0.61;
    std::cout << "Kills: " << kills << "\n";
    std::cout << "Accuracy: " << accuracy << " (" << accuracy * 100 << "%)\n";
}
```

```text
Kills: 25
Accuracy: 0.61 (61%)
```

### How it works

- `#include <iostream>` brings in the stream library (C++ standard headers have no `.h`).
- `std::cout` is the **standard output** stream, the C++ equivalent of `stdout`.
- `<<` sends a value into the stream. Expressions chain from left to right: each `<<` returns the stream again, so the next `<<` continues writing.
- There are **no format specifiers**. The compiler knows each value's type and picks the right way to print it, so the classic `printf` mismatch bugs can't happen.
- `std::` is a **namespace** prefix: the standard library's names live in the namespace `std`, so they don't clash with your own names.
- In C++, `main` may leave out `return 0;`; reaching the end of `main` means success.

You'll see `std::endl` in older code; it prints a newline **and** flushes the stream, which is slower. `"\n"` is usually what you want.

steps.title: Formatting tables with iomanip
steps.text:
Printing numbers in neat columns needs control over **width**, **alignment** and **decimal places**. In C that's `printf("%-10s%6.2f")`. In C++ it's the manipulators from `<iomanip>`:

| Manipulator | Effect |
|---|---|
| `std::setw(n)` | pad the **next** item to width n (only the next one!) |
| `std::left`, `std::right` | alignment inside that width (sticky) |
| `std::fixed` + `std::setprecision(2)` | always 2 digits after the decimal point (sticky) |
| `std::setfill('0')` | pad with a character other than space (sticky) |

"Sticky" settings stay on the stream until you change them. `setw` resets after each item.

```cpp
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2);
    std::cout << std::left << std::setw(8) << "item" << std::right << std::setw(8) << "price" << "\n";
    std::cout << std::left << std::setw(8) << "tea" << std::right << std::setw(8) << 3.5 << "\n";
    std::cout << std::left << std::setw(8) << "cake" << std::right << std::setw(8) << 12.999 << "\n";
    std::cout << std::setfill('0') << std::setw(2) << 7 << ":" << std::setw(2) << 5 << "\n";
}
```

```text
item       price
tea         3.50
cake       13.00
07:05
```

### Reading the example

- `std::fixed << std::setprecision(2)` is set once at the top and applies to every floating point number after it. Without `std::fixed`, `setprecision(2)` would mean "2 significant digits" and print `3.5` as `3.5` and `12.999` as `13`.
- `std::setw(8)` is written **before every item** that needs padding, because it only lasts for one item.
- `std::left` and `std::right` are sticky, so a table that mixes alignments has to switch back and forth, as each row does here.
- `12.999` rounds to `13.00`: `setprecision` rounds, it never just chops digits off.
- If a value is **wider** than the `setw`, it's printed in full; the column just gets pushed over. Nothing is ever cut off.

### The K/D detail in your task

`kills / deaths` with two `int`s does integer division. Convert one side first: `static_cast<double>(kills) / d`. And handle the "0 deaths counts as 1" rule before dividing.

**Your turn:** read `name kills deaths` rows and print a table: name left-aligned in 10 columns, kills and deaths right-aligned in 4 columns each, then the K/D ratio right-aligned in 6 columns with 2 decimals (use 0 deaths as 1 death).
hints: Set `std::fixed << std::setprecision(2)` once before the loop; they're sticky.
Per row: `std::left << std::setw(10) << name`, then `std::right` and `std::setw(4)` before kills, again before deaths, `std::setw(6)` before the ratio.
Compute the ratio as a double: `static_cast<double>(kills) / (deaths == 0 ? 1 : deaths)`.

require.message: Line up the columns with `std::setw`.

modules.title: Design patterns in modern C++
modules.summary: The patterns you'll meet in every large C++ codebase, written the modern way. Strategies as closures, a factory registry, observers with weak_ptr, pimpl, RAII wrappers for C libraries, and a table-driven state machine.

steps.title: Strategies as closures
hints: `return [pct](long cents) { return cents - cents * pct / 100; };`
flat_off: return 0 when the amount is bigger than the total.
total(): sum the prices, then `return discount(sum);`

steps.title: A factory registry

create: `find` the name; if missing return nullptr, otherwise call the creator: `it->second()`.

`Roster::Roster() : impl_(std::make_unique<Impl>()) {}`, and `Roster::~Roster() = default;` after Impl is defined.

steps.title: RAII wrappers for C libraries
hints: `struct FileCloser { void operator()(std::FILE* f) const { if (f) std::fclose(f); } };`
`using File = std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser>;` and open_file returns `File(std::fopen(path.c_str(), mode))`.

handle: ask next(); if it's empty return false, otherwise update the state and count.

modules.title: Complexity and searching
modules.summary: Big-O in practice. Trading memory for speed with hash sets, binary search and lower_bound, two pointers, prefix sums and sliding windows, with tests big enough that slow solutions time out.

steps.title: Big-O in practice
hints: Keep a `std::unordered_set<int> seen;`.
`seen.insert(x).second` is false when x was already there. That's your duplicate.

steps.title: Binary search
hints: Track an inclusive range `lo..hi`, starting at 0 and size - 1.
`int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;` then move lo to `mid + 1` or hi to `mid - 1`.
The loop runs while `lo <= hi`; if it ends, the target isn't there.

forbid.message: Write the halving loop yourself on this step.

steps.title: lower_bound and upper_bound
hints: `auto first = std::lower_bound(sorted.begin(), sorted.end(), lo);`
`auto last = std::upper_bound(sorted.begin(), sorted.end(), hi);` and return `last - first`.

require.message: Use `std::lower_bound` and `std::upper_bound` so each query is O(log n).

steps.title: Two pointers
hints: Start `i = 0` and `j = size - 1`, and loop while `i < j`.
Add as long to avoid overflow; move i up when the sum is too small, j down when too big.

steps.title: Prefix sums
hints: Store `std::vector<long long> pre_` with one more slot than the input, starting at 0.
`pre_[i + 1] = pre_[i] + v[i];` then `sum(l, r)` is `pre_[r + 1] - pre_[l]`.

steps.title: Challenge: sliding window
hints: Keep `std::array<int, 256> last` filled with -1: the last index where each byte was seen.
For each right: if `last[c] >= left`, move `left = last[c] + 1`. Then record `last[c] = right`.
The window length is `right - left + 1`; keep the maximum.

modules.title: Sorting algorithms
modules.summary: How sorting really works. Insertion sort, merge sort, quicksort partitioning, counting sort, stability with custom comparators, and quickselect.

steps.title: Insertion sort
hints: Loop i from 1; save `key = v[i]` and slide j down while `v[j - 1] > key`.
Using `j > 0` with `v[j - 1]` avoids a negative size_t index.
Count one shift each time you copy `v[j] = v[j - 1]`.

forbid.message: Implement the algorithm yourself on this step.

steps.title: Merge sort
hints: Write a recursive helper that sorts the half-open range `[lo, hi)` using one shared temporary buffer.
Base case: fewer than 2 elements. Otherwise sort `[lo, mid)` and `[mid, hi)`, then merge into tmp and copy back.
When merging, take from the right half only if it's strictly smaller; that keeps the sort stable.

forbid.message: Implement merge sort yourself on this step.

steps.title: Quicksort and partitioning
hints: partition: `int pivot = v[hi]; int i = lo;` then for each j < hi, swap smaller elements to position i.
Finally swap the pivot into place: `std::swap(v[i], v[hi]); return i;`
quick_sort: stop when `lo >= hi`, else partition and recurse on both sides of p.

forbid.message: Implement the partition yourself on this step.

steps.title: Counting sort
hints: `std::vector<int> count(max_value + 1, 0);` and `count[x]++` for every x.
Then walk value from 0 to max_value, writing it `count[value]` times.

forbid.message: Count, don't compare, on this step.

steps.title: Stability and custom comparators
hints: Use `std::stable_sort` with a lambda comparator.
Highest first: `return a.score > b.score;`

forbid.message: A comparator must be strict: use `>` or `<`, never `<=` or `>=`.

steps.title: Challenge: quickselect
hints: Loop with a range `[lo, hi]`. Swap the middle element to hi and partition like Lomuto.
After partitioning, the pivot is at its final index i. If k == i you're done; otherwise narrow the range to the side containing k.
When lo == hi, that single element is the answer.

forbid.message: Write the partition loop yourself.

modules.title: Hash tables
modules.summary: Build the data structure behind unordered_map. Buckets and chaining, load factor and rehashing, a string-keyed map with erase, custom hashes for your own keys, and an LRU cache.

steps.title: Buckets and chaining
hints: Write a helper: `std::size_t bucket_of(int key) const { return std::hash<int>{}(key) % buckets_.size(); }`
insert: search that bucket's list with `std::find`; if absent, push_back and grow size_.
contains: same search, return whether it was found.

forbid.message: Build it from buckets yourself on this step.

steps.title: Load factor and rehashing
hints: After a successful insert, check `size_ * 4 > buckets_.size() * 3` (0.75 without floating point).
rehash: swap the buckets into a local `old`, give buckets_ twice as many empty lists, then re-insert every key from old.
Swapping first means bucket_of() already uses the new bucket count while re-inserting.

forbid.message: Grow your own table on this step.

steps.title: A string-keyed map with erase
hints: Each bucket is a list of `std::pair<std::string, int>`. Find the bucket with `std::hash<std::string>{}(key) % buckets_.size()`.
put: if the key is in the bucket, overwrite `.second`; otherwise `emplace_back(key, value)`.
get returns `&kv.second` for a match. erase walks with an iterator and calls `b.erase(it)`.

forbid.message: Build the map from your own buckets on this step.

steps.title: Hashing your own keys
hints: PointHash combines the two int hashes with the formula shown above.
`std::unordered_set<Point, PointHash> seen{{0, 0}};` starts with the origin.
After each move, `if (!seen.insert(p).second) count++;`

steps.title: Challenge: an LRU cache
hints: get: find the key in where_; if found, `items_.splice(items_.begin(), items_, it->second)` and return the value.
put on an existing key: update the value and splice it to the front.
put on a new key: `emplace_front`, record `where_[key] = items_.begin()`, and if over capacity erase `items_.back()` from both structures.

modules.title: Trees and heaps
modules.summary: Recursive thinking with trees. Binary tree basics, binary search trees, traversals and validation, level-order with a queue, a binary heap by hand, and a trie for autocomplete.

steps.title: Binary trees and recursion
hints: Base case: `if (!n) return 0;`
height is 1 + the larger of the two subtree heights; sum is the value plus both subtree sums.
Use `.get()` to pass a child's raw pointer without giving up ownership.

steps.title: Binary search trees
hints: Walk a pointer-to-slot down from `&root_`; stop at an empty slot.
Go left when `key < (*slot)->key`, right when greater, and return false on equality.
contains is the same walk with a plain `const Node*`.

steps.title: Traversals and validation
hints: in_order: recurse left, push the key, recurse right.
is_bst: an empty subtree is fine. Otherwise the key must satisfy lo < key < hi.
Going left tightens the upper bound to the key; going right tightens the lower bound.

steps.title: Level order with a queue
hints: Use `std::queue<const Node*>` starting with the root.
Each round, read `q.size()` first, then pop exactly that many nodes into one level vector, pushing their children.

steps.title: A binary heap by hand
hints: push: append, then while i > 0 and the parent `(i - 1) / 2` is bigger, swap and move up.
pop: move the last element to index 0, pop_back, then sift down.
Sift down: find the smallest of i, 2i+1 and 2i+2 (those that exist); stop if it's i, else swap and continue.

forbid.message: Implement the sift-up and sift-down loops yourself on this step.

steps.title: Challenge: a trie for autocomplete
hints: insert: skip if already contained. Walk from the root creating missing children, incrementing `pass` on every node (including the root).
Write a private `find(prefix)` that returns the node at the end of the prefix, or nullptr.
complete: from that node, depth-first over children 0..25, appending letters to a running string and collecting words where `end` is true, until you have `limit`.

modules.title: Graphs
modules.summary: Model connections. Adjacency lists, breadth-first shortest paths on a grid, depth-first flood fill, topological sort for build order, Dijkstra with a priority queue, and union-find.

steps.title: Adjacency lists
hints: `Graph adj(n);` then for each edge `adj[a].push_back(b);` and, if undirected, the reverse.
max_degree is the largest `adj[v].size()`.

steps.title: Shortest path with BFS
hints: Keep `dist` as a grid of -1 (unvisited). Find S, set its distance to 0 and push it.
Pop the front; if it's E return its distance. Otherwise push each in-bounds, non-wall, unvisited neighbor with distance + 1.
If the queue empties first, return -1.

steps.title: Depth-first flood fill
hints: Scan every cell. When you find a `#`, count a new island and flood it.
Flood with a vector used as a stack: mark cells as visited (turn them into '.') when you push them, so none is pushed twice.
Taking the grid by value lets you modify your own copy.

steps.title: Topological sort
hints: Build an adjacency list and an in-degree count from the dependency pairs.
Seed a `std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>>` with all in-degree-0 vertices.
Pop, append, decrement dependents, push any that hit 0. Return {} if the order is shorter than n.

steps.title: Dijkstra's shortest paths
hints: Build an adjacency list of (neighbor, cost) pairs.
Use a min-heap of (distance, vertex): `std::priority_queue<Item, std::vector<Item>, std::greater<Item>>`.
Skip popped entries whose distance is larger than the best known one; relax each edge and push improvements.

steps.title: Challenge: union-find
hints: Store `parent_` (initialized to 0..n-1 with std::iota), `size_` (all 1) and a group counter.
find: walk up to the root, then walk again pointing every node on the path straight at the root.
unite: find both roots; if equal return false. Attach the smaller root under the larger, add sizes, decrement groups.

modules.title: Capstone: code review
modules.summary: Review realistic pull requests the way a senior engineer would. Each step hides several real bugs (off-by-one errors, dangling references, leaks on error paths, invalidated iterators, integer overflow and broken class design) for you to find and fix.

steps.title: Review: pagination
hints: Bug 1: page is 1-based, so page 1 must start at index 0: `(page - 1) * per_page`.
Bug 2: the last page can be partial, and pages past the end are empty. Clamp `end` to `items.size()`.
Bug 3: invalid arguments. Reject `page < 1 || per_page < 1` up front. And `page * per_page` can overflow an int: compute it in `long long`.

steps.title: Review: dangling references
hints: `greeting` returns a view of the local `text`, which is destroyed at the closing brace. Return `std::string` instead.
`Tag` stores a view of the temporary string built in `make_tag`. Make the member a `std::string`; the accessor can still return a view of it.

steps.title: Review: leaks on the error path
hints: Leak 1: when strtol fails, `return -1` skips freeing `values`.
Leak 2: when n == 0, the early return skips freeing both buffers.
One tidy fix: keep a `result` variable, `goto cleanup;` on errors, and free both pointers (xfree(nullptr) is safe) at a single `cleanup:` label.

steps.title: Review: modifying while iterating
hints: Bug 1: after `erase(begin() + i)`, the next player moves into slot i and `i++` skips them. `std::erase_if` (C++20) removes all matches correctly and returns how many.
Bug 2: the second loop push_backs into `roster` while range-for iterates it. Just loop `removed` times instead.
Bug 3: `captain` is a reference into the vector, and push_back may reallocate. Copy the string instead.

forbid.message: `captain` is a reference into the vector, and push_back can reallocate and leave it dangling. Copy the name first.

steps.title: Review: integer math
hints: win_rate: guard `games <= 0`, and do the multiplication in `long long`: 1.5 billion × 100 doesn't fit in an int.
average: an empty vector divides by zero, and an `int` sum overflows for big scores. Use a long long sum and check empty first.
last_n_total: `scores.size() - n` is unsigned, so it wraps to a huge number when n is bigger than the size. Clamp the start index.

steps.title: Review: class design
hints: Make the base destructor `virtual`, so deleting a Sniper through a Weapon pointer runs ~Sniper.
`int damage()` in Sniper lacks `const`, so it doesn't override. Add `const override` (and `override` on name()).
`std::vector<Weapon>` slices every Sniper into a plain Weapon. Take `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Weapon>>` and call `w->name()`.

projects.summary: Read expressions like `3 + 4`, handle every operator, refuse division by zero, and keep going until the user types q.

milestones.title: Add two numbers
milestones.text:
Read two numbers from input and print their sum with two decimals.

Input:
```
3 4.5
```
Output:
```
7.50
```

Use `scanf("%lf %lf", &a, &b)` to read two doubles, then `printf("%.2f\n", a + b)`.
hints: `%lf` reads a double with scanf. Don't forget the `&` before each variable.
`%.2f` prints a number with exactly two digits after the decimal point.

milestones.title: Pick the operator
milestones.text:
Now the input includes an operator between the numbers: `+`, `-`, `*` or `/`.

```
6 * 7
```
prints `42.00`.

Read the operator with `%c`. Put a space before it in the format (`" %c"`) so scanf skips the space after the first number.
hints: `scanf("%lf %c %lf", &a, &op, &b)` reads number, operator, number.
A `switch (op)` with `case '+':` etc. keeps it tidy. Remember `break;` after each case.

milestones.title: Guard against bad input
milestones.text:
Two things can go wrong:

- Dividing by zero should print `error: division by zero`
- An unknown operator like `%` should print `error: unknown operator %`

Everything else works as before.
hints: Check `b == 0` inside the `/` case before dividing.
The `default:` case of a switch runs when no other case matches.

milestones.title: Keep calculating until q
milestones.text:
Turn it into a loop. Keep reading expressions and printing results until the input line is just `q`.

```
1 + 1
5 / 0
2 * 3
q
```
prints
```
2.00
error: division by zero
6.00
```

Tip: `scanf` returns how many values it read. `scanf("%lf %c %lf", &a, &op, &b)` returns 3 for a full expression, but when it meets `q` it can't read a number, so it returns 0. Loop while it returns 3 and the `q` ends the loop for you.
hints: Put the scanf call in the loop condition: `while (scanf("%lf %c %lf", &a, &op, &b) == 3)`.
The division-by-zero and unknown-operator cases now print their error and carry on to the next line, so replace their `return 0` with `break` (which leaves the switch, not the loop).

milestones.title: Your own random secret
milestones.text:
Real games pick the secret randomly. `rand()` gives different numbers on different systems, so you'll write your own tiny **linear congruential generator** (LCG), the same kind many C libraries use internally:

```c
unsigned int state = seed;
state = state * 1103515245u + 12345u;     // wraps around at 2^32
int secret = (int)((state / 65536u) % 100u) + 1;
```

`unsigned int` is an integer type that can't be negative; read it with `%u`. When unsigned arithmetic goes past the largest value it wraps around to 0 and keeps counting (well defined, unlike signed overflow), which is exactly what an LCG needs.

Now the first line of input is a **seed** instead of the secret. Compute the secret from it with one LCG step.

Also limit the player to **7 attempts**. After the 7th wrong guess print `out of guesses, it was N` and stop. (Running out of input still prints `out of guesses, it was N`.)
hints: Read the seed with `%u` into an `unsigned int`. Unsigned arithmetic wraps around cleanly at 2^32.
Add `attempts < 7 &&` to the loop condition (before the scanf, so no extra guess is read).
With seed 1, the secret is 60.

projects.title: Build your own dynamic array
projects.summary: Write the growable array every language hides from you. malloc, realloc doubling, insert, remove and shrink, all tested by hidden unit tests.

milestones.title: New, push, get, free
milestones.text:
You're writing a library, so there's no `main`: hidden tests call your functions.

- `vec_new()` returns an empty vector with **capacity 4** (allocate the storage).
- `vec_push(v, x)` appends `x`. When `size == cap`, **double** the capacity with `realloc` first.
- `vec_get(v, i)` returns element `i` (you can assume `i` is valid).
- `vec_free(v)` frees the storage and sets `data` to NULL, size and cap to 0.
hints: vec_new: set cap to 4, size to 0, and `data = malloc(cap * sizeof(int))`.
vec_push: if `v->size == v->cap`, grow into a temporary first: `int *bigger = realloc(v->data, 2 * v->cap * sizeof(int));`. Only if it isn't NULL, store it in `v->data` and double `v->cap`.
Then `v->data[v->size++] = x;`

milestones.title: Pop and remove
milestones.text:
Add:

- `int vec_pop(IntVec *v)` removes and returns the last element (assume non-empty)
- `int vec_remove(IntVec *v, int i)` removes element `i`, shifts everything after it one place left, and returns the removed value
hints: pop: `return v->data[--v->size];`
remove: save the value, then shift `data[k] = data[k + 1]` for k from i up to size - 2, and decrease size.

milestones.title: Insert
milestones.text: Add `void vec_insert(IntVec *v, int i, int x)` that inserts `x` **before** index `i` (0 to size; inserting at `size` appends). Grow first if full, then shift elements right, starting from the end.
hints: Grow the same way push does.
Shift from the back: `for (int k = v->size; k > i; k--) v->data[k] = v->data[k - 1];`

milestones.title: Reserve and shrink
milestones.text:
Finish the library with capacity control:

- `void vec_reserve(IntVec *v, int cap)` grows the capacity to at least `cap` (never shrinks)
- `void vec_shrink(IntVec *v)` reduces the capacity to exactly `size` (but at least 1)

Both use `realloc`.
hints: reserve: return early if `cap <= v->cap`.
shrink: the target capacity is size, or 1 when empty.

projects.title: Matrix library
projects.summary: A Matrix class with operators for addition, scaling, multiplication, transpose, printing and a determinant.

milestones.title: Storage and access
milestones.text:
Store the elements in one `std::vector<double>` in **row-major** order: element `(r, c)` lives at index `r * cols + c`.

Implement:

- `Matrix(int rows, int cols)` creates a zero-filled matrix
- `int rows() const`, `int cols() const`
- `double& at(int r, int c)` and `double at(int r, int c) const`
hints: Initialize `data_(rows * cols, 0.0)` in the initializer list.
`return data_[r * cols_ + c];`

milestones.title: Add, compare, scale
milestones.text:
Add non-member operators:

- `Matrix operator+(const Matrix& a, const Matrix& b)` (same size assumed)
- `bool operator==(const Matrix& a, const Matrix& b)` (same size and all elements equal)
- `Matrix operator*(const Matrix& m, double k)` (scale every element)
hints: Build a result matrix of the same size and fill it with nested loops.
For ==, compare sizes first, then every element.

milestones.title: Matrix multiplication
milestones.text:
Add `Matrix operator*(const Matrix& a, const Matrix& b)`: an `n x m` times an `m x p` gives an `n x p` matrix where

```
out(r, c) = sum over k of a(r, k) * b(k, c)
```

Also add a static `Matrix::identity(int n)` returning the `n x n` identity matrix (1 on the diagonal).
hints: The result has a's rows and b's columns.
Three nested loops. The innermost sums `a.at(r, k) * b.at(k, c)`.
`static Matrix identity(int n)` goes inside the class.

milestones.title: Transpose and printing
milestones.text:
Add:

- `Matrix transpose() const` (rows become columns)
- `std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream&, const Matrix&)` that prints each row on its own line, elements separated by single spaces, e.g. `1 2 3`. Print numbers with plain `<<` (so 2.5 prints as `2.5` and 3.0 prints as `3`).
hints: transpose: result is cols x rows with `t.at(c, r) = at(r, c)`.
operator<<: a space before every element except the first in each row, then `'\n'`.

milestones.title: Determinant
milestones.text:
Add `double determinant() const` for square matrices. The recursive **cofactor expansion** along the first row is the easiest to write:

```
det([a]) = a
det(M) = sum over c of (-1)^c * M(0, c) * det(minor(0, c))
```

where `minor(0, c)` is M without row 0 and column c. (It's slow for big matrices, and that's fine here.)
hints: Base case 1x1 returns the element.
For each column c of row 0: build the minor by copying rows 1..n-1 and skipping column c.
Alternate the sign: + for even c, - for odd c.

projects.title: Your own vector<T>
projects.summary: Re-implement std::vector as a class template. Growth, deep copies, moves, iterators, so it works with range-for and std::sort.

milestones.title: Grow and index
milestones.text:
Build `Vec<T>` step by step. Storage is a raw array from `new T[cap]`, released with `delete[]`. (That requires `T` to be default-constructible. The real `std::vector` uses lower-level tricks to avoid that; you don't need them here.)

Implement:

- a default constructor (empty, no allocation) and a destructor
- `void push_back(const T& x)`: when full, grow capacity to `cap == 0 ? 1 : cap * 2`, allocate a new array, **move** the old elements across, delete the old array
- `std::size_t size() const`, `std::size_t capacity() const`
- `T& operator[](std::size_t i)` and a const version

For now, delete the copy operations (`Vec(const Vec&) = delete;` and the same for `operator=`) so nothing copies by accident.
hints: A private helper `void grow(std::size_t new_cap)` keeps push_back short.
In grow: `T* fresh = new T[new_cap];` move elements with `fresh[i] = std::move(data_[i]);`, then `delete[] data_; data_ = fresh;`.

milestones.title: Deep copies
hints: Copy constructor: allocate `new T[other.size_]` (or nullptr when empty) and copy element by element.
Copy assignment takes its parameter **by value**, then swaps. The parameter's destructor frees the old contents.

milestones.title: Moves
milestones.text:
Add a move constructor. It steals the pointer and leaves the source empty (`nullptr`, size 0, capacity 0). Mark it `noexcept`.

You don't need a separate move assignment. Because copy assignment takes its parameter by value, `a = std::move(b)` move-constructs that parameter (cheap now) and swaps. In fact, adding `Vec& operator=(Vec&&)` next to `Vec& operator=(Vec)` makes `a = std::move(b)` ambiguous, and it won't compile.
hints: `Vec(Vec&& other) noexcept : data_(other.data_), size_(other.size_), cap_(other.cap_) { ...reset other... }`

milestones.title: Iterators, back and pop_back
milestones.text:
Make `Vec` work with range-for and the standard algorithms by adding iterators. For a contiguous array, plain pointers **are** iterators:

```cpp
T* begin() { return data_; }
T* end() { return data_ + size_; }
```

Add const versions too, plus `T& back()`, `void pop_back()` and `bool empty() const`.

Then `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end())` and `for (auto& x : v)` just work.
hints: `T* begin() { return data_; }` and `T* end() { return data_ + size_; }`, plus const overloads returning `const T*`.
`back()` is `data_[size_ - 1]`; `pop_back()` just decrements size_.

projects.title: Expression interpreter
projects.summary: A calculator language with precedence, parentheses, variables and error messages. Tokenizer, recursive-descent parser and evaluator, no exceptions.

milestones.title: Plus and minus
milestones.text:
Each input line is an expression of integers with `+` and `-`, spaces optional. Print its value.

```
1 + 2 - 3 + 10
100-1
42
```
prints
```
10
99
42
```

Walk the string with an index. Skip spaces, read a number digit by digit, then repeatedly read an operator and another number.
hints: A small struct holding the string and a position `i` keeps the parsing functions tidy.
`number()`: skip spaces, then `v = v * 10 + (s[i++] - '0')` while the char is a digit.
`expr()`: read a number, then loop: if the next char is + or -, consume it, read another number and combine.

milestones.title: Precedence
milestones.text:
Add `*` and `/` (integer division), which bind tighter than `+` and `-`. The classic **recursive descent** grammar:

```
expr   = term   { ("+" | "-") term }
term   = factor { ("*" | "/") factor }
factor = number
```

Each rule becomes a function that calls the next one down.

`2 + 3 * 4` prints `14`; `20 / 3 * 3` prints `18`.
hints: An `eat(char c)` helper that skips spaces and consumes c if it's next makes every rule shorter.
term() is just like expr() but with * and /, and it calls factor() instead of term().

milestones.title: Parentheses and unary minus
milestones.text:
Extend `factor`:

```
factor = number | "(" expr ")" | "-" factor
```

`(2 + 3) * 4` prints `20`; `-(4 - 10)` prints `6`; `--3` prints `3`.
hints: factor() now checks three cases: a `-` (negate the next factor), a `(` (parse a whole expr, then eat `)`), or a number.
Calling expr() from factor() is fine. That mutual recursion is what makes nesting work.

milestones.title: Variables
milestones.text:
Add variables stored in a `std::map<std::string, long long>` (or unordered_map):

- `let NAME = EXPR` stores the value and prints `NAME = VALUE`
- a name inside an expression is replaced by its value

Names are letters and underscores. The map must survive from line to line.

```
let hp = 100
let dmg = 27 * 2
hp - dmg
```
prints
```
hp = 100
dmg = 54
46
```
hints: Check whether the line starts with `let ` before parsing an expression.
In factor(): if the next char is a letter or `_`, read a name and return its value from the map.
The map lives outside the loop (a global or a variable in main passed to the parser).

projects.title: Write a memory allocator
projects.summary: See what malloc does underneath. A bump allocator with alignment, then a fixed-size pool allocator built on a free list.

milestones.title: Bump allocator
milestones.text:
The simplest allocator hands out memory from one big array by moving a pointer forward ("bumping" it). It can't free individual blocks, only reset everything at once. Game engines use exactly this for per-frame scratch memory.

- `void *bump_alloc(size_t n)` returns `heap + used` and advances `used` by `n`. If fewer than `n` bytes are left, return `NULL` and change nothing.
- `void bump_reset(void)` makes all 4096 bytes available again.
hints: Bytes left are `sizeof(heap) - used`. Compare with that (not `used + n > 4096`) to avoid overflow.
Return `heap + used` before advancing.

milestones.title: Alignment
milestones.text:
CPUs want an `int` at an address divisible by 4, a `double` by 8, and so on. `malloc` guarantees suitably aligned memory, so yours should too.

Round every request **up to a multiple of 8** before bumping, so every returned address is 8-aligned (the heap itself starts 16-aligned):

```c
size_t rounded = (n + 7) & ~(size_t)7;
```

Also make `bump_alloc(0)` return `NULL`.
hints: `(n + 7) & ~(size_t)7` clears the low 3 bits after adding 7, rounding up to a multiple of 8.
Use the rounded size for both the space check and the bump.

milestones.title: A pool with a free list
milestones.text:
A **pool allocator** hands out blocks of one fixed size, and *can* free them individually. The trick: free blocks store a pointer to the next free block **inside themselves**, forming a linked list that costs zero extra memory.

```c
#define BLOCK 16
#define BLOCKS 32
static _Alignas(16) unsigned char pool[BLOCK * BLOCKS];
static void *free_list = NULL;
```
