topics.title: Operator overloading in C++
topics.description: Make your types work with +, ==, <<, [] and more, with the conventions that keep overloaded operators unsurprising.
topics.body:
You can define what operators mean for your own types, so a `Vec2` can be added with `+` and printed with `<<`.

Guidelines:

- Only overload an operator when its meaning is obvious (math types, containers, comparisons).
- Implement `+=` as a member and `+` in terms of it.
- `operator<<` for printing takes `std::ostream &` and returns it, so calls can chain.
- In C++20, `bool operator==(const T &) const = default;` and `auto operator<=>(const T &) const = default;` generate comparisons for you.

topics.title: std::vector in C++
topics.description: How to use std::vector, the dynamic array of C++, plus size vs capacity, reserve, and iterator invalidation.
topics.body:
`std::vector<T>` is a resizable array that manages its own memory. It's the default container in C++: fast to iterate, indexable in O(1), and `push_back` is amortized O(1).

- `v.size()` is how many elements there are; `v.capacity()` is how many fit before it must grow.
- When it grows, it moves everything to a bigger block, which invalidates pointers and iterators into it. `reserve(n)` avoids repeated growth when you know the size.
- `v[i]` doesn't check bounds; `v.at(i)` does.
- Loop with `for (const auto &x : v)`.

topics.title: std::map and std::unordered_map
topics.description: Key-value lookups in C++, the difference between map and unordered_map, and the operator[] insertion trap.
topics.body:
Both store key-value pairs with unique keys:

| | `std::map` | `std::unordered_map` |
|---|---|---|
| Built on | balanced tree | hash table |
| Lookup | O(log n) | O(1) on average |
| Order | sorted by key | none |

Use `unordered_map` for fast lookups and `map` when you need keys in order. Watch out: `m[key]` **inserts** a default value if the key is missing. To check without inserting, use `m.contains(key)` (C++20) or `m.find(key)`.

topics.title: Lambdas in C++
topics.description: Writing lambda functions in C++, capture by value and by reference, and using lambdas with STL algorithms.
topics.body:
A lambda is an unnamed function you can write inline: `[capture](parameters) { body }`.

The capture list decides which outside variables it can use:

- `[x]` copies `x` when the lambda is created.
- `[&x]` refers to the real `x` (it must outlive the lambda).
- `[=]` and `[&]` capture everything used, by copy or by reference.

Lambdas are most useful as arguments to algorithms like `std::sort`, `std::count_if` and `std::transform`.

topics.title: STL algorithms in C++
topics.description: sort, find, count_if, accumulate, transform and friends, and why algorithms beat hand-written loops.
topics.body:
`<algorithm>` and `<numeric>` hold dozens of tested building blocks that work on any range:

- `std::sort`, `std::stable_sort`
- `std::find`, `std::find_if`, `std::count_if`, `std::any_of`
- `std::accumulate` (sum or fold), `std::transform` (map)
- `std::lower_bound` (binary search on sorted data)
- `std::erase_if` (C++20) to remove matching elements

Using a named algorithm says what the code does, and avoids off-by-one mistakes. C++20 ranges let you pass the container directly: `std::ranges::sort(v)`.

topics.title: Smart pointers: unique_ptr, shared_ptr and weak_ptr
topics.description: How C++ smart pointers own heap objects and free them automatically, and when to use each one.
topics.body:
Smart pointers own a heap object and delete it for you:

- `std::unique_ptr<T>`: exactly one owner. Can't be copied, only moved. Zero overhead. **The default choice.** Make one with `std::make_unique<T>(args)`.
- `std::shared_ptr<T>`: shared ownership with a reference count; the last owner deletes it. Use only when ownership is genuinely shared.
- `std::weak_ptr<T>`: watches a shared object without keeping it alive, to break reference cycles.

With smart pointers and containers, modern C++ code almost never calls `new` or `delete` directly.

topics.title: Move semantics and std::move
topics.description: What moving means in C++, rvalue references, what std::move really does, and the rule of five.
topics.body:
Copying a `std::vector` of a million elements copies a million elements. **Moving** it just hands over the internal buffer pointer, and in practice leaves the source empty. That's why returning big objects by value is cheap in modern C++.

A class supports moving with a **move constructor** `T(T &&other) noexcept` and **move assignment**. `std::move(x)` doesn't move anything itself: it's a cast that says "you may steal from x". After a move, only assign to or destroy the source.

Mark move operations `noexcept`, or `std::vector` will copy instead of move when it grows (for any type that can be copied).

topics.title: Templates in C++
topics.description: Function and class templates in C++, type deduction, and constraining templates with C++20 concepts.
topics.body:
A template is a blueprint the compiler fills in for each type you use it with. `std::vector<int>` and `std::vector<std::string>` are two different classes generated from one template.

Function templates usually deduce their types from the arguments: `max_of(3, 7)` uses `T = int`.

C++20 **concepts** state what a template needs, such as `template <std::integral T>`, which gives far clearer error messages than the old walls of template errors.

topics.title: Inheritance and virtual functions in C++
topics.description: Base and derived classes, virtual functions and override, abstract classes, and why virtual destructors matter.
topics.body:
A derived class inherits from a base class and can **override** its `virtual` functions. Calling a virtual function through a base pointer or reference runs the version for the object's real type: that's **runtime polymorphism**.

- Write `override` on overrides so the compiler catches signature mistakes.
- A pure virtual function (`= 0`) makes the class abstract: an interface that can't be instantiated.
- Give a polymorphic base class a `virtual` destructor, or deleting through a base pointer is undefined behavior.
- Pass polymorphic objects by reference or pointer; passing by value **slices** off the derived part.

topics.title: Modern C++: C++17 and C++20 features
topics.description: The modern C++ features worth knowing, from auto and structured bindings to std::optional, concepts and ranges.
topics.body:
Modern C++ (C++11 onward, and especially C++17 and C++20) is much friendlier than older styles:

- `auto` type deduction and range-based `for`
- **structured bindings**: `auto [key, value] = pair;`
- `std::optional<T>` for "a value or nothing"
- `std::variant` for "one of these types"
- `std::string_view` and `std::span` for non-owning views
- C++20: **concepts**, **ranges**, `<=>` comparisons, `std::format`

Together with smart pointers and RAII, these let you write code that is both fast and hard to misuse.

topics.title: Error handling in C and C++
topics.description: Return codes, errno, exceptions, std::optional and std::expected, and how to choose between them.
topics.body:
There are several ways to report that something failed:

- **Return codes** (C style): return -1 or `NULL` and set `errno`. Simple, but easy to ignore.
- **Exceptions** (`throw` / `try` / `catch`): errors can't be silently ignored, and RAII cleans up as the stack unwinds. Standard C++ uses them for truly exceptional failures.
- **`std::optional<T>`**: "a value or nothing", when the reason doesn't matter.
- **`std::expected<T, E>`** (C++23): a value or an error explaining why.

Whatever you pick, be consistent within a codebase, and never let a failure pass silently.

topics.title: Big-O notation explained
topics.description: What O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) and O(n^2) mean, with examples of each, for coding interviews and real code.
topics.body:
Big-O describes how an algorithm's work grows as the input grows, ignoring constant factors:

| Big-O | Name | Example |
|---|---|---|
| O(1) | constant | index into an array, hash lookup |
| O(log n) | logarithmic | binary search |
| O(n) | linear | scan a list once |
| O(n log n) | linearithmic | good sorting algorithms |
| O(n^2) | quadratic | nested loops over the same data |

For a million items, O(n^2) means about a trillion steps while O(n log n) is about 20 million. Picking the right data structure usually matters more than micro-optimizing code.

topics.title: Binary search
topics.description: How binary search finds a value in sorted data in O(log n), how to write it without bugs, and std::lower_bound.
topics.body:
Binary search works on **sorted** data. Compare the target with the middle element; if the target is bigger, it can only be in the right half, so discard the left half, and vice versa. Each step halves the range, so a million elements take about 20 comparisons.

Classic bugs: computing `(lo + hi) / 2` can overflow for huge indexes (use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`), and off-by-one loop bounds. In C++, prefer `std::lower_bound`, which returns the first position not less than the target.

topics.title: Sorting algorithms compared
topics.description: Insertion sort, merge sort, quicksort and counting sort compared by speed, memory and stability.
topics.body:
| Algorithm | Average | Worst | Stable | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Insertion sort | O(n^2) | O(n^2) | yes | fast for small or nearly sorted data |
| Merge sort | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | yes | needs O(n) extra memory |
| Quicksort | O(n log n) | O(n^2) | no | fast in practice, in place |
| Counting sort | O(n + k) | O(n + k) | yes | small integer keys only |

**Stable** means equal elements keep their original order, which matters when sorting by one field after another. In real code, use `std::sort` (an introsort hybrid, never O(n^2)) or `std::stable_sort`.

topics.title: How hash tables work
topics.description: Hash functions, buckets, collisions, chaining and load factor, the ideas behind std::unordered_map.
topics.body:
A hash table turns a key into a number with a **hash function**, then uses that number to pick a **bucket**. Looking up the key means hashing it again and checking only that bucket, which is why lookups are O(1) on average.

Two keys can land in the same bucket (a **collision**). With **chaining**, each bucket holds a small list. The **load factor** (items divided by buckets) is kept low by growing the table and rehashing everything when it gets too full.

A bad hash function that sends many keys to one bucket turns lookups into O(n) scans.

topics.title: Binary trees and binary search trees
topics.description: Tree terminology, recursive traversals, and how binary search trees keep data sorted for O(log n) lookups.
topics.body:
In a **binary tree** each node has up to two children. In a **binary search tree** (BST), everything in a node's left subtree is smaller than it and everything in its right subtree is larger, so a lookup walks down one path.

Traversals visit every node, usually recursively:

- **in-order** (left, node, right) visits a BST in sorted order
- **pre-order** (node first) and **post-order** (children first, useful for freeing)
- **level order** uses a queue to go row by row

An unbalanced BST can degrade into a list; `std::map` uses a self-balancing tree to guarantee O(log n).

topics.title: Graphs: BFS and DFS
topics.description: Representing graphs with adjacency lists, and exploring them with breadth-first and depth-first search.
topics.body:
A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges. The usual representation is an **adjacency list**: for each node, a list of its neighbors (`std::vector<std::vector<int>>`).

- **Breadth-first search (BFS)** uses a queue and visits nodes in order of distance, so it finds shortest paths when every edge has the same cost.
- **Depth-first search (DFS)** uses recursion or a stack and goes as deep as possible first; it's used for cycle detection and topological sorting.

Both mark nodes as visited so they're processed once, giving O(V + E) time.
